name: edges of a broken concrete pavement area laid on dirt: the cracked concrete pads break into the dirt in small irregular chunks with a subtle darker lip under the break, with outer and inner corners, the full interior filled with the cracked concrete slab field
label: wasteland_ruins/slab-edge

surfaces.part: concrete pad chunks on dirt (flat ground terrain tiles)

answer.evidence: This is a terrain autotile sheet: cracked concrete patches on a dirt background, with edge, corner and full-interior variants. The silhouette is a full 256-wide block on every row, so there is no standing object. The concrete is drawn as flat ground seen from above. The only vertical-looking detail is a thin darker lip under the broken edges, 1-2 rows tall, which reads as ground relief, not a front face. Terrain is judged as flat ground, so there is no top plus front structure and no front face of 3 or more rows.

styleAnswer.evidence: The measured facts are acceptable. The candidate has 5 visible tones per tile against 7 for the paving reference and 3 for the grass reference. Near-flat coverage is 1%, and the dark edge pixels are tinted (0% neutral), so there is no black sticker line. The craft is still shallow by eye. The concrete reads as only about 3 greys (light, mid, speckle) and the dirt as about 3 browns, with 12 distinct colours in the whole piece. The paving reference has roughly 6-7 steps with per-stone shading and clear highlight and shadow edges. The candidate's concrete chunks are speckled but have no highlight-to-deep ramp. The darker lip under the break is faint and not a distinct shadow step. The large slab on the right is mostly one mid grey with sparse crack lines. Overall the pieces look like pale cut-outs on a busy dirt field, thinner and flatter than the Beodeul reference. When in doubt, fail.

surfaces.part: cracked concrete pads on dirt (terrain field)

answer.evidence: This is a flat terrain tile sheet seen from straight above: a dirt ground with irregular grey concrete patches, which include strips, corners, a small chunk and a large filled slab. The silhouette is a full 256-wide opaque rectangle on every row, and there is no standing volume. The darker lip under the breaks is a 1-row shadow on the ground, not a front face. No part of it shows a raised top surface or a vertical south face of 3 or more rows, so as a terrain tile it reads as a flat top-down slab.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate has only 12 distinct colours and 5 visible tones per tile (references: 3 for grass, 7 for paving). The grey concrete ramp has about 3 steps (light grey, mid grey, a few darker speckles) against the 5-6 steps Beodeul uses per material. The dirt ramp is also about 3 steps of brown with scattered dark pebbles. Texture is speckle noise, with no per-chunk highlight and shadow, and no stones shaded one by one like the paving reference. Near-flat coverage is low (1%), so there are no flat fills. Dark edge pixels are tinted (0% neutral), but the concrete edges have no clear darker lip under the break, so the outline is mixed and mostly separated by value alone. The brief asked for a 4x3 patch with edge, corner and interior pieces. The board shows scattered blobs and one rectangular slab with a few cracks, so the structure is less complete and less crafted. Overall it reads thinner and flatter than the references, a little short of the Beodeul bar.

surfaces.part: cracked concrete pavement patches on dirt (flat ground terrain)

answer.evidence: This is a terrain tile sheet: a flat dirt field with grey cracked-concrete patches. The silhouette is a full 256-wide block on every row, with no standing volume. The concrete patches are flat ground seen from above. Their breaks into the dirt have only a thin darker lip of 1 row or less, not a vertical front face of 3 or more rows. The column scan shows only alternating dirt tones and a short concrete run (rows 51-57). No eave line, ellipse, or roof plane appears. It is ground texture with no front face, so it reads as flat top-down terrain.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a brown dirt field with grey concrete patches. The dirt has speckled grain, but the concrete pads are shaded with only about 3 grey steps: a light grey body, a few lighter and darker dots, and a faint dark lip. The 12 distinct colours overall are fewer than the paving reference's 7 visible tones per tile suggests it needs, and the candidate shows 5 visible tones per tile against the reference's 7. The concrete is the object the brief is about, and it reads as thin. The chunks look like isolated cut-out blobs rather than a coherent edge set. The large slab at right has only a few thin cracks, a pale lighter rim and no per-slab highlights or stone-by-stone shading, so it is flatter than the paving reference. The edge pixels are tinted, with 0% near-neutral, so there is no black sticker outline. Overall it has some texture but shallow shading, lower density, and a weaker structure than the reference, so it fails.

surfaces.part: cracked concrete pads (edge, corner and full slab pieces)

answer.evidence: This is a terrain autotile sheet seen from directly above: dirt fills the whole 256x192 canvas, with grey cracked concrete patches (T-shaped strip, L-shaped strip, a small square, a large slab with crack lines, and small irregular chunks). The patches are flat ground and have no front face. Each has only a thin darker lip at its lower break edge, 1-2 rows, which reads as a shadow rim and not as a vertical face of 3 or more rows. The column scan shows repeating tile bands of the same colors every 64 rows, which confirms this is a flat tiling ground texture. Terrain tiles are meant to be flat, so there is no standing volume to measure.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate has only 12 distinct colours in total, split across dirt and concrete, so each material ramp has about 3-4 steps against Beodeul's 5-6. The concrete is a mid grey with a lighter speckle and a thin darker lip, and the dirt is a brown mottle with a few darker dots. The dark edge pixels are tinted (0% neutral), so the outline reads as a dark material tone and not a black sticker line. There are 5 visible tones per tile, which is below the paving reference's 7 and above the grass reference's 3. Near-flat coverage is 1%, so there are no big flat fills. Even so, the concrete chunks are small and softly stippled, with little per-chunk shading and a simple cracked-slab interior. The slab pieces also look scattered on the dirt and do not read as a rich, shaded edge set with a full slab field. Overall it is competent but shallower and flatter than the Beodeul references, so I fail it under the 'when in doubt, fail' rule.
